title: Authentication vs authorization
objectives: Define authentication as proving identity and authorization as granting capability after identity is known.
Separate MFA, SSO/identity-provider login, and session security from user permissions, profiles, and permission sets.
Diagnose a login failure versus a permission failure without collapsing the problem into record sharing or organization-wide defaults.
Explain why an established session is not itself a permission grant.
diagnostic_question: LAB_Rep can open Salesforce after MFA, but cannot View Setup. A teammate wants to 'raise the session timeout so they get admin rights.' What is authentication here, what is authorization, and which layer would you change first?
definition: Authentication is the process of validating that a user is who they say they are before they log in, perform an action, or access information. Authorization is what they are allowed to do after identity is proven: user permissions, profiles, and permission sets grant tasks and features. A session is the authenticated connection that follows login; session settings limit exposure of that connection. They do not replace permission grants. ([MFA Glossary](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.mfa_glossary.htm); [User Permissions](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=admin_userperms.htm); [Session Security](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.security_overview_sessions.htm))
why_it_matters: Interviewers listen for whether you treat a login failure like a missing permission, or a missing permission like an MFA problem. Mixing those layers burns time, over-grants privileges, or leaves a user locked out. Least privilege in the MFA glossary is an authorization idea: the fewest permissions necessary to do the job. MFA is an authentication control that does not give those permissions.
sixty_second_explanation: Think of a concert venue. Authentication is the ID check at the door, including a second factor like a wristband scanner. Authorization is the ticket type: general admission versus backstage. After you are inside, the venue stamp on your hand is the session; when it fades you prove identity again. The stamp does not upgrade you to backstage. Record sharing, which decides which seats you can walk to, is a later SEC topic.
deeper_explanation: The MFA glossary defines authentication as validating that a user is who they say they are. Multi-factor authentication requires two or more pieces of evidence from different categories (something the user knows, has, or is). Salesforce requires MFA for user-interface logins. MFA does not grant View Setup, Modify All Data, or any other user permission. ([MFA Glossary](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.mfa_glossary.htm))

User permissions specify what tasks users can perform and what features they can access, for example View Setup and Configuration or API Enabled. Salesforce recommends permission sets and permission set groups as reusable authorization building blocks so you do not create dozens of profiles per job. That is authorization, not identity proof. ([User Permissions](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=admin_userperms.htm))

In SAML single sign-on, the identity provider authenticates the user (confirms who they are). After that, it sends a SAML assertion to the service provider about who the user is. Salesforce can be the identity provider or the service provider. SSO is still an authentication path; the org still authorizes with permissions after the user lands. ([SAML SSO Flows](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.identity_provider_about.htm))

After login, the user establishes a session. Session security limits exposure when someone walks away still logged in, and it can require a High Assurance session for sensitive operations. The documented default inactivity timeout is two hours unless the org changes Session Settings. A longer session does not grant extra user permissions. ([Session Security](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.security_overview_sessions.htm))

Do not collapse this lesson into organization-wide defaults, role hierarchy, or sharing rules. Those answer which records a user can reach after they are authenticated and authorized to use the object. SEC-003 and SEC-004 own that stack.

mental_model.analogy: A concert venue: door ID plus a second factor is authentication; ticket type is authorization; the fading hand stamp is the session.
useful_mapping: ID check at the door → authentication (username/password, SSO, identity provider)
second scanner or authenticator app → MFA verification method
ticket type (GA vs backstage) → user permissions, profiles, permission sets
hand stamp that expires → session, timeout, session security level
which seats you can walk to after you are inside → record sharing (later SEC topics)
where_it_breaks: A SAML assertion can carry attributes about what the user may do at the service provider; that does not replace Salesforce permission sets inside the org.
High-assurance session policies can gate sensitive operations, which feels like authorization but is still a session-security control on an already authenticated user.
The venue does not model organization-wide defaults or sharing rules.

teach_back_prompt: Without using the words authentication or authorization until the last sentence, explain why MFA cannot give LAB_Rep View Setup, and why extending session timeout cannot either.

review_schedule.prompt: From memory, write authentication vs authorization, then name MFA, identity provider, session, and user permission in one sentence each.
Classify four tickets: cannot log in, MFA prompt loop, missing View Setup, cannot see a peer Opportunity.
Explain why a session is not a permission, using the Session Security Help idea of timeout and high assurance.
Walk a SAML identity-provider flow and say what is proven versus what Salesforce still authorizes locally.
Two-minute interview: authentication vs authorization, plus one sharing-boundary you refuse to mix in.

interview_explanation.thirty_seconds: Authentication proves identity: password, MFA, SSO identity provider. Authorization grants capability: user permissions via permission sets or profiles. A session is the authenticated connection after login. I do not treat sharing or OWD as this lesson.
interview_explanation.two_minutes: I split a ticket before I touch Setup. If the user cannot log in, I stay on authentication: credentials, MFA verification method, identity provider, then session timeout if they were in and got dropped. If they are in and cannot perform a task, I look at user permissions, not MFA. Least privilege is an authorization design. Record sharing answers which records they reach and belongs to later SEC topics.

terminology.plain: Proving the person is who they claim to be.
terminology.precise: The process of validating that a user is who they say they are before they log into an account, perform an action, or access information.
terminology.example: LAB_Rep completes username, password, and an authenticator-app challenge, then reaches the Lightning home page.
terminology.non_example: Assigning the View Setup and Configuration user permission is authorization, not authentication.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Authorization: what the proven user may do.
terminology.boundary: This lesson stops before record sharing and OWD.

terminology.plain: What a proven user is allowed to do.
terminology.precise: Capability granted after identity is known, expressed as user permissions, profiles, and permission sets for tasks and features.
terminology.example: LAB_Admin has View Setup and Configuration in a permission set so they can open Setup.
terminology.non_example: Completing MFA does not, by itself, grant View Setup.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Record-level sharing: which records, not which tasks.
terminology.boundary: Object, field, and record layers are SEC-002 through SEC-004.

terminology.plain: Login that needs more than one kind of proof.
terminology.precise: A security measure that requires two or more pieces of evidence from different categories during login. Salesforce also calls this a verification-method requirement; 2FA is a deprecated term at Salesforce.
terminology.example: Password (something you know) plus Salesforce Authenticator (something you have).
terminology.non_example: Two passwords of the same category are not MFA as defined in the glossary.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: High-assurance session: a session security level after login, not the MFA definition itself.
terminology.boundary: MFA configuration details continue in SEC-007.

terminology.plain: The system that confirms who you are in an SSO flow.
terminology.precise: In SAML SSO, the identity provider authenticates the user and sends a signed SAML response. Salesforce can be the identity provider or the service provider.
terminology.example: Users authenticate at a corporate IdP, then land in Salesforce as the service provider.
terminology.non_example: A permission set is not an identity provider.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Service provider: the app that consumes the assertion after authentication.
terminology.boundary: Connected-app OAuth details belong with later identity and integration topics.

terminology.plain: The authenticated connection that exists after a successful login.
terminology.precise: After logging in, a user establishes a session with the platform. Session security settings control timeout, connection behavior, and session security levels such as Standard or High Assurance.
terminology.example: An inactive session hits the org timeout and the user is prompted to continue or log out.
terminology.non_example: Lengthening session timeout does not grant API Enabled or View Setup.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: User permission: a durable authorization grant, not a timed connection.
terminology.boundary: Login hours and IP ranges are SEC-007; this lesson only needs session ≠ permission.

terminology.plain: A named task or feature the user may use.
terminology.precise: User permissions specify what tasks users can perform and what features they can access. They are enabled in permission sets and custom profiles.
terminology.example: API Enabled on a permission set so an integration user can call APIs.
terminology.non_example: An MFA verification method is not a user permission.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Object permission: CRUD on an object, taught in SEC-003.
terminology.boundary: Least privilege in the MFA glossary is the design rule for these grants.

terminology.plain: Give only the access the job needs.
terminology.precise: The idea that a user should have the fewest number of permissions necessary to do their job, and nothing more.
terminology.example: LAB_Rep gets sales permissions, not Customize Application.
terminology.non_example: Cloning System Administrator because login failed.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: MFA: reduces account-takeover risk; it is not a substitute for least-privilege permissions.
terminology.boundary: Sharing least privilege is later; here it means permission grants.

mechanics.failure: Treating a password/MFA failure as a missing permission set

mechanics.failure: Assuming the session itself grants Setup or API rights

mechanics.after: Allowed or denied by user permissions
mechanics.observe: Permission set or profile includes or lacks the permission

when_to_use: When an interview asks you to separate authentication from authorization in Salesforce identity work.
When a user cannot log in, loops on MFA, or fails an identity-provider SSO redirect.
When a logged-in user lacks a task or feature such as View Setup, and you must inspect user permissions rather than MFA.
When someone proposes session timeout, session security level, or a longer session as a substitute for a permission set.
when_not_to_use: Do not use this authentication vs authorization lesson to design organization-wide defaults, role hierarchy, or sharing rules (SEC-004).
Do not treat MFA or an identity provider as a way to grant object, field, or record access.
Do not use session settings to authorize privileged users; session security limits an authenticated connection.
Do not collapse user-permission troubleshooting into page-layout or sharing checks before you have named the authorization grant.
configuration_or_code_location: Setup → Identity, MFA, and Single Sign-On related pages for authentication paths.
Setup → Session Settings and Session Management for the authenticated connection.
Setup → Permission Sets / Profiles for user permissions (authorization).
Setup → Identity Provider when Salesforce is the SAML identity provider.

worked_example.scenario: In a disposable LAB_ org, LAB_Rep completes MFA and reaches Lightning but cannot open Setup. A manager asks to extend session timeout and to 'turn off MFA for admins so they get more access.' No production users.

A request to lengthen session timeout

decisions.decision: Treat the Setup gap as authorization, not authentication.
decisions.because: The user already proved identity; User Permissions Help is the layer for tasks and features.
decisions.rejected: Disable MFA or raise session timeout to 'give admin rights'

decisions.decision: Grant the minimum user permission via a permission set if policy allows Setup access at all.
decisions.because: Help recommends permission sets and permission set groups over proliferating profiles, and least privilege forbids cloning System Administrator.
decisions.rejected: Clone System Administrator because login succeeded

decisions.decision: Leave Opportunity sharing and OWD unchanged.
decisions.because: The symptom is a feature (Setup), not a missing record.
decisions.rejected: Open OWD Public Read/Write as a side effect

configuration_or_code: Confirm LAB_Rep has an active session after MFA (authentication succeeded).
Inspect LAB_Rep's permission sets for View Setup and Configuration.
If the lab policy allows it, assign a narrow LAB_Setup_Read permission set; do not disable MFA.
Leave Session Settings at the documented org value unless you are testing timeout as a separate hypothesis.
worked_example.output: LAB_Rep remains MFA-authenticated. Setup appears only after the user permission is present. Session timeout is unchanged. OWD is untouched.
verification: LAB_Rep can log in with MFA before and after the permission change.
Setup is visible only when View Setup and Configuration is enabled.
Session timeout was not used as the authorization fix.
worked_example.self_explanation: Identity was already proven. I authorized a task with a user permission. I refused to treat session or MFA as capability.

hands_on_lab.environment: Disposable Developer sandbox or Trailhead Playground; synthetic LAB_ users only.
starting_state_checks: You can create a LAB_ user and a permission set.
steps: Create LAB_Rep with a standard sales-style profile that does not include View Setup.
Log in as LAB_Rep and confirm authentication succeeds (complete any MFA the org requires).
Attempt Setup as LAB_Rep and record the failure as an authorization miss.
Assign a permission set that includes only the lab-approved Setup permission, then retest as LAB_Rep.
Write one sentence: session timeout was not the fix; sharing was not the fix.
guided_completion: If LAB_Rep still cannot log in, you are still on authentication.
If LAB_Rep is in but cannot open Setup, name the user permission you inspected.
hands_on_lab.independent_challenge: A teammate wants High Assurance session settings to replace a permission set. Explain why that is the wrong layer.
evidence: Notes showing login succeeded before the permission change.
Permission set assignment for LAB_Rep with LAB_ names only.
stop_recovery_cleanup: Deactivate LAB_Rep and remove the lab permission set.
Do not disable org MFA as part of this exercise.
hands_on_lab.limitations: This lab does not configure a production identity provider or change org-wide Session Settings.

decision_table.signal: User never reaches Lightning; MFA or SSO challenge fails.
decision_table.choose: Authentication path: credentials, MFA verification method, identity provider.
decision_table.not: A new permission set or profile clone.
decision_table.why: Identity is not proven yet; user permissions are not evaluated as the first fix.

decision_table.signal: User was working, then an inactivity prompt logs them out.
decision_table.choose: Inspect session timeout and Session Settings as session security.
decision_table.not: Grant extra user permissions so they 'stay admin longer'.
decision_table.why: Session Security Help treats timeout as exposure control on an authenticated connection.

decision_table.signal: User is logged in but cannot perform View Setup or API Enabled.
decision_table.choose: Authorization: user permission on a permission set or custom profile.
decision_table.not: Disable MFA or raise High Assurance to mimic a privilege grant.
decision_table.why: User Permissions Help is the task-and-feature layer; MFA is still authentication.

decision_table.signal: User can use Opportunities generally but cannot open one peer-owned record.
decision_table.choose: Stop this lesson and move to record-level access (SEC-003/SEC-004).
decision_table.not: Change MFA, session timeout, or identity-provider settings.
decision_table.why: Authentication and user-permission authorization already succeeded; sharing is a later stack.

limitations: Does not configure login hours, IP ranges, or connected-app OAuth (SEC-007).
Does not design OWD, roles, or sharing rules.
MFA product enforcement and available verification methods are org- and product-specific.
security_notes: Least privilege is an authorization rule; MFA is not a substitute for it.
Never disable MFA in production to 'grant access'.
Do not log session IDs, passwords, or verification codes in lab notes.
common_mistakes: Saying MFA is an authorization tool.
Equating a session with a permission set.
Fixing a missing record with an identity-provider change.
Cloning System Administrator because login succeeded.

That MFA completed (proves you are past authentication).

mcqs.prompt: According to the MFA glossary, what is authentication?

options.A: Validating that a user is who they say they are before login, an action, or access
options.B: Granting the fewest object permissions needed for a job
options.D: Extending session timeout to two days

mcqs.rationale: The glossary defines authentication as validating identity before login, action, or access.

distractor_explanations.B: That is least privilege, an authorization idea.
distractor_explanations.C: OWD is record sharing, not this lesson.
distractor_explanations.D: Timeout is session security, not the definition of authentication.

options.A: What tasks users can perform and what features they can access

mcqs.rationale: User Permissions Help states they specify tasks and features, such as View Setup or API Enabled.

distractor_explanations.C: IdP signing is an SSO implementation detail.

mcqs.prompt: What happens after a user logs in, according to Session Security Help?

options.A: The user establishes a session with the platform
options.C: All user permissions become System Administrator
options.D: Organization-wide defaults reset to Public Read/Write

mcqs.rationale: After logging in, a user establishes a session. Session settings then control that connection.

distractor_explanations.B: MFA is not disabled by creating a session.
distractor_explanations.D: Sharing is unrelated to session creation.

mcqs.prompt: In a SAML flow, what does the identity provider do first?

options.A: Authenticate the user (confirm they are who they say they are)
options.D: Create a High Assurance session without login

mcqs.rationale: SAML SSO Flows: the identity provider authenticates the user, then sends a SAML response.

distractor_explanations.B: Salesforce still authorizes locally with permissions.
distractor_explanations.C: OWD is not an IdP job.
distractor_explanations.D: A session follows successful login, it is not a substitute for authentication.

mcqs.prompt: LAB_Rep completed MFA and is in Lightning but cannot View Setup. What layer is this?

options.A: Authorization: a user permission is missing
options.C: Session: timeout must be increased to grant Setup
options.D: Sharing: OWD must be Public Read/Write

mcqs.rationale: Identity is proven. View Setup is a user permission (authorization).

distractor_explanations.D: Setup access is not a record-sharing problem.

mcqs.prompt: What is the documented default inactivity session timeout in Session Security Help?

options.D: Timeout equals the user's profile login hours

mcqs.rationale: Help states the default session timeout is two hours of inactivity. Orgs can change Session Settings.

distractor_explanations.D: Login hours are a later SEC-007 control.

mcqs.prompt: How does Salesforce Help recommend managing users' permissions?

options.A: Use permission sets and permission set groups as reusable building blocks
options.B: Create a unique profile for every user
options.D: Grant Modify All Data via session timeout

mcqs.rationale: User Permissions Help recommends permission sets and permission set groups to avoid dozens or hundreds of profiles.

distractor_explanations.B: That is the anti-pattern Help warns against.
distractor_explanations.C: MFA is authentication, not a permission model.
distractor_explanations.D: Sessions do not grant Modify All Data.

mcqs.prompt: A manager wants to turn off MFA so support agents 'get more permissions.' What do you say?

options.A: MFA proves identity; it does not grant user permissions
options.B: Turning off MFA automatically assigns permission set groups
options.C: MFA is the same as organization-wide defaults

mcqs.rationale: MFA is authentication. Least privilege still governs authorization separately.

distractor_explanations.B: MFA and permission sets are different layers.

mcqs.prompt: Which request should you refuse to solve inside this authentication vs authorization topic?

options.A: Peers cannot see each other's Opportunities; please change OWD
options.C: Users lack the API Enabled user permission
options.D: SSO identity provider is not returning a SAML assertion

mcqs.rationale: OWD and record sharing are later SEC topics. The other options are authentication or user-permission authorization.

distractor_explanations.C: API Enabled is a user permission.

mcqs.prompt: How is a High Assurance session different from a user permission?

options.A: Session security level can gate resources for an already authenticated user; a user permission is the durable task/feature grant
options.D: User permissions expire every two hours by default

mcqs.rationale: Session Security Help describes Standard vs High Assurance session levels. User permissions remain the authorization catalog.

distractor_explanations.C: MFA is a login factor; high assurance is a session level.
distractor_explanations.D: The two-hour figure is session inactivity timeout, not permission expiry.

mcqs.prompt: Least privilege in the MFA glossary refers to what?

options.A: The fewest number of permissions necessary to do the job
options.B: Using only one MFA verification method

mcqs.rationale: The glossary defines least privilege as fewest permissions necessary, limiting impact of errors and compromised credentials.

distractor_explanations.B: Users can register multiple verification methods as backups.
distractor_explanations.C: That is the opposite of least privilege for records.
distractor_explanations.D: SSO is an authentication design, not least privilege.

mcqs.prompt: Salesforce is configured as a SAML identity provider for a benefits app. What did Salesforce prove when the user logged in to that app?

options.A: Identity (authentication) to the service provider via a signed SAML response
options.B: That the user has Modify All Data in every Salesforce org
options.C: That Opportunity sharing rules were copied to the benefits app
options.D: That session timeout in Salesforce is now infinite

mcqs.rationale: When Salesforce is the IdP, it authenticates the user and signs the SAML response for the service provider.

distractor_explanations.C: Sharing does not travel with SAML as OWD.

interview_questions.question: Explain authentication vs authorization in Salesforce.
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Authentication proves identity: password, MFA, SSO identity provider. Authorization is what the proven user may do: user permissions via permission sets or profiles. A session is the connection after login, not a permission.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I start with the MFA glossary: authentication validates that the user is who they say they are. MFA adds a second factor from another category. After login, Session Security Help says a session is established; timeout and high assurance protect that session. User Permissions Help is authorization: tasks and features such as View Setup or API Enabled, preferably via permission sets. I explicitly do not fold OWD or sharing into this answer.
interview_questions.example: LAB_Rep completes MFA (authentication) but still cannot View Setup until a permission set grants that user permission (authorization).
tradeoffs: SSO convenience vs still managing Salesforce permissions

interview_questions.question: Why is a Salesforce session not a permission?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: A session is the authenticated connection after login. Session settings control timeout and security level. User permissions still decide tasks and features.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: Session Security Help exists to limit exposure when someone walks away still logged in, and to apply Standard vs High Assurance levels. Lengthening timeout keeps the same identity online longer; it does not add View Setup. I would inspect Session Management to see that a session exists, then inspect permission sets for capability. Mixing the two is a common interview fail.
interview_questions.example: A manager asks to raise timeout so LAB_Rep 'becomes admin.' I refuse and look at user permissions instead.
tradeoffs: Usability of longer sessions vs exposure
High-assurance gates vs durable permission grants

When would you require High Assurance?

interview_questions.question: A user cannot log in. Another user logs in but cannot open Setup. How do you split the tickets?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Cannot log in is authentication: credentials, MFA, identity provider. Logged in without Setup is authorization: View Setup and Configuration on a permission set or profile.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I refuse a single 'access' ticket. For login I ask whether a session is ever created. For Setup I confirm MFA already succeeded so identity is proven. Then I look at user permissions, not sharing. If they can use the object but not one record, I park that for SEC-003/004. Least privilege still applies: I will not clone System Administrator to clear either ticket.
interview_questions.example: LAB_Rep MFA works; Setup fails until a narrow permission set is assigned. LAB_NewHire never passes the authenticator challenge, so no permission work yet.
tradeoffs: Speed of cloning an admin profile vs least privilege
Treating all access tickets as sharing
follow_ups: What if SSO is in the path?

interview_questions.question: Stakeholders want MFA disabled for admins so privileged users 'have more access.' Respond.
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: I would not disable MFA to grant access. MFA is identity proof. Privileged users still need least-privilege permissions, and they are high-value authentication targets.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: The MFA glossary defines privileged users as admins and users with high access, including people with Customize Application or Modify All Data. That is why authentication should be stronger, not weaker. Authorization is a separate permission-set design. I would also note Salesforce requires MFA for UI logins; I would not promise a production exemption. Session high-assurance can add another gate after login, still without replacing permissions.
interview_questions.example: LAB_Admin keeps MFA and receives only the Setup permissions the job needs, not a blanket System Administrator clone.
tradeoffs: Friction of MFA vs account-takeover risk
follow_ups: How do you handle SSO MFA?
weak_answer_warnings: Agreeing to disable MFA as an authorization shortcut

interview_questions.question: Where does SAML identity provider fit relative to Salesforce permission sets?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: The identity provider authenticates. Salesforce permission sets still authorize tasks in the org after the user lands, unless a later identity topic owns Just-in-Time provisioning details.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: SAML SSO Flows: the IdP confirms who the user is and sends a signed assertion. Salesforce may be IdP or service provider. I treat that as the authentication path. I still inspect profiles and permission sets for API Enabled or View Setup. I do not claim the assertion replaced sharing or OWD. If attributes drive provisioning, I mark mapping details as Needs verification in the target org rather than inventing JIT behavior.
interview_questions.example: Corporate IdP logs LAB_Rep into Salesforce; they still need a sales permission set to work Opportunities as a feature, and sharing still decides which Opportunities.
tradeoffs: Central IdP vs local Salesforce authorization
Assertion attributes vs explicit permission sets
follow_ups: What is signed in the SAML response?

interview_questions.question: A user says Salesforce 'keeps logging them out' and they want System Administrator. Diagnose.
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: I check whether this is session timeout versus missing permissions. Inactivity timeout is session security. System Administrator is an authorization nuclear option I will not use to fix timeout.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I reproduce: if they were in the app and got the inactivity dialog, I look at Session Settings. Help documents a default two-hour inactivity timeout; I reverify the org value. If they cannot perform a task while the session is active, I inspect user permissions. I keep MFA in place. I do not open sharing. I explain least privilege: timeout and admin rights solve different risks.
interview_questions.example: LAB_Rep hits the timeout prompt after idle time; granting View Setup would not stop the prompt, and cloning System Administrator would over-authorize.
follow_ups: Where do you see active sessions?
What is High Assurance used for?

interview_questions.question: How do you keep record sharing out of an authentication vs authorization interview answer?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: I say sharing answers which records after identity and object capability are known. If the user cannot log in or lacks a user permission, I do not touch OWD.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I use a three-bucket model: prove identity, grant tasks/features, then later decide records. Interviewers often bait you into OWD during an auth question. I name the bait: peers missing an Opportunity is SEC-004. Missing View Setup is a user permission. Failed MFA is authentication. That discipline shows I will not over-share to fix a login, or over-authenticate to fix a record.
interview_questions.example: Ticket: LAB_Rep cannot see LAB_Opportunity_Orion. I first confirm they can log in and have Opportunity Read. Only then do I leave this topic for sharing analysis.
tradeoffs: Complete access-path answers vs topic boundaries
follow_ups: What is the next topic after user permissions?
Where do object CRUD and FLS sit?
weak_answer_warnings: Opening with OWD on an MFA question

interview_questions.question: Teach authentication vs authorization to a new admin using a concrete analogy, then break it.
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Concert venue: ID plus a second factor is authentication; ticket type is authorization; the fading stamp is the session. The analogy breaks because a SAML assertion can carry extra attributes, and high-assurance sessions can gate operations.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I walk LAB_Rep through the door. MFA is the second scanner. Permission sets are the ticket type. Session timeout is the stamp fading. I then say what the venue cannot model: Salesforce user permissions live in permission sets and profiles; identity providers authenticate; sharing is which seats. I finish with least privilege: a backstage ticket is not issued because someone passed the ID check. That is the interview-ready close.
interview_questions.example: LAB_Rep passes MFA, still has a general-admission permission set, and is not given System Administrator because the stamp lasted two hours.
tradeoffs: Memorable analogy vs precise Help wording
Teaching speed vs over-extending the metaphor
follow_ups: Where does High Assurance sit in the analogy?
weak_answer_warnings: Using a labeled-drawer or library filler analogy
Never stating where the analogy breaks
